lesson_title: Comparing RC Low-Pass and High-Pass Filters
lesson_core_move: Distinguish RC low-pass and high-pass filters by comparing their magnitude-response trends to predict which frequency components are passed or attenuated.

images.section_title: Introduction to Comparing RC Low-Pass and High-Pass Filters
images.image_description: A clean textbook-style plot on shared axes comparing normalized RC magnitude responses. The low-pass curve should start near 1 at low frequency and fall toward 0 at high frequency. The high-pass curve should start near 0 at low frequency and rise toward 1 at high frequency. Include a cutoff marker, label the low-frequency and high-frequency ends, and keep the figure schematic and uncluttered.

outline_section.section_title: Introduction to Comparing RC Low-Pass and High-Pass Filters
outline_section.learning_goal: Introduce the endpoint-comparison rule for reading RC low-pass and high-pass magnitude responses.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean comparison plot of normalized RC magnitude responses on shared axes, showing a low-pass curve that is high at low frequency and falls toward high frequency, and a high-pass curve that is low at low frequency and rises toward high frequency.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a textbook-style schematic with minimal visual clutter. Emphasize the opposite endpoint trends of the two filters rather than exact numeric values.

question_policy.answer_format: No practice questions for the tutorial section.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the learner to compare the low- and high-frequency endpoints of the RC low-pass and high-pass magnitude responses and use that comparison to predict pass or attenuation.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with one component well below cutoff and one component well above cutoff so each endpoint trend is obvious before moving to mixed cases.
paragraph_plan: State the comparison rule up front: this lesson is about reading magnitude-response trends, not about re-deriving the circuits.
Use the low-frequency endpoint to show why the RC low-pass passes a slowly varying component and the RC high-pass attenuates it.
Use the high-frequency endpoint to show the opposite behavior.
Compress the two checks into one reusable rule for later examples: larger magnitude means the component is passed more strongly.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Anchor the lesson with one comparison visual, then move immediately into low-frequency and high-frequency endpoint rules before any practice.

images.section_title: Identifying Filter Type from a Magnitude Response
images.image_description: A clean schematic magnitude-response plot for an RC filter with frequency on the horizontal axis and normalized magnitude on the vertical axis. The single response curve starts near 0 at low frequency, rises smoothly across a cutoff marker, and ends near 1 at high frequency. Keep the plot uncluttered, with clear axes and minimal labels beyond the curve trend.

image_slot.image_description: A clean schematic magnitude-response plot for an RC filter with frequency on the horizontal axis and normalized magnitude on the vertical axis. The single response curve starts near 0 at low frequency, rises smoothly across a cutoff marker, and ends near 1 at high frequency. Keep the plot uncluttered, with clear axes and minimal labels beyond the curve trend.

outline_section.section_title: Identifying Filter Type from a Magnitude Response
outline_section.learning_goal: Identify RC low-pass versus high-pass behavior from the shape of a magnitude-response plot.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A single magnitude-response plot for an RC filter with frequency on the horizontal axis and normalized magnitude on the vertical axis, where the curve either falls from left to right or rises from left to right so the learner can identify the filter type.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the plot uncluttered and schematic. The practice questions should reuse the same visual style with different curve directions or cutoff locations.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices naming the filter type from the plot.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a magnitude-response plot, decide whether the filter is RC low-pass or RC high-pass by reading the low-frequency and high-frequency ends of the curve.
distractor_plan: Reverse the slope and pick the opposite filter.
Treat a high left endpoint as evidence for high-pass.
Treat a low left endpoint as evidence for low-pass.
Use cutoff location alone instead of endpoint trend.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: From the given magnitude-response plot, identify whether the filter is RC low-pass or RC high-pass by comparing the low-frequency and high-frequency ends of the curve.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map the visual trend to filter identity.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Convert the endpoint rule into an image-reading task.
solution_step_plan: Read the low-frequency end of the plot.
Read the high-frequency end of the plot.
Match the trend to low-pass or high-pass behavior.
practice_variation_axes: Vary how steeply the curve transitions.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Treat the plot as the problem data; keep the answer choices textual, but require fresh plot images in the follow-up questions.

prompt_blocks.text: Which RC filter type matches the response curve shown?

choice_blocks.text: Cannot be determined from the cutoff marker alone

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The curve starts low on the left and ends high on the right, which matches the RC high-pass pattern. The endpoint trend, not the cutoff marker alone, identifies the filter type.
